1	Reasoning models with chain-of-thought (CoT) can self-jailbreak: their reasoning traces transition from safe deliberation to committed harmful generation without adversarial input. We define the commitment point (CP) as the first reasoning step after which safety deliberation permanently ceases, and provide initial characterization of hidden-state (HS) vs.\ text probes for CP detection across four reasoning LLMs (3 Qwen-family, 1 Llama) on HarmThoughts. The comparison depends critically on which transformer layer is monitored---a known sensitivity in probing~\citep{belinkov2022probing} that we show is severe enough to reverse conclusions in the safety domain: a crossing-rate composite metric masks the HS advantage at 32B scale by selecting shallow layers where representation compression inflates threshold crossings. Threshold-based layer selection recovers HS precision gains of +15.4 to +21.9pp against a 384d distilled sentence encoder (Holm-Bonferroni corrected; upper bound), but this advantage is doubly conditional: it diminishes with stronger text encoders (4/4 HB at 384d $\to$ 1/4 at 1024d) and partially overlaps with temporal position. The 7--8B results are validated via nested 5-fold CV; the 32B results ($n \leq 20$) are exploratory. Seven alternative methods (change-point detection, geometric distance, representation engineering, cross-model transfer) all fail to match supervised probing. Metric-induced layer selection bias is the robust methodological finding; the empirical HS advantage is conditional on encoder quality, model scale, and position control.

Reasoning models such as DeepSeek-R1~\cite{deepseekr1} and QwQ~\cite{qwq} scale inference-time computation through extended chains of thought (CoT). Recent work documents that these models can ``self-jailbreak'': without adversarial input modification, the CoT transitions from safety-aware deliberation to committed harmful generation~\cite{harmthoughts,selfjailbreak}. We define the first reasoning step after which safety deliberation permanently ceases as the \textbf{Safety Commitment Point} (CP). This failure mode differs qualitatively from adversarial jailbreaks on standard LLMs because the harmful transition originates within the model's own reasoning. Recent work shows that chain-of-thought faithfulness is limited~\citep{chen2025unfaithful}, motivating hidden-state monitoring that bypasses surface text. Before retrospective characterization can inform future detection systems, a prior question must be answered: can current probing methods reliably distinguish pre-CP from post-CP reasoning steps, and under what conditions? This paper provides \emph{retrospective} classification (not online detection) of what hidden-state and text-based probes can and cannot detect; false positive rates remain 11--50\%, so deployment applications are future work.\looseness=-1

Existing safety detectors target fundamentally different problems. Hidden-state (HS) methods such as TrajGuard~\cite{trajguard} and SafeSwitch~\cite{safeswitch} classify adversarial inputs at the token level, while text monitors like SafeRemind~\cite{saferemind} scan generated reasoning for explicit violations. Neither tracks the gradual, multi-step commitment process. HS probes require choosing which transformer layer to monitor, a researcher degree of freedom typically treated as a minor implementation detail. Before asking which modality is better, a prior methodological question must be answered: how sensitive are probe conclusions to the choice of layer selection metric? We show this choice alone can reverse a study's central conclusion: the same data yield a 14-layer (R1-8B) to 61-layer (QwQ-32B) divergence depending solely on metric choice; for QwQ-32B, at threshold-based layers the HS advantage is +19pp ($p{<}0.005$); at crossing-rate-selected layers, it is non-significant ($p{=}0.83$). Prior hidden-state probing targets standard LLMs~\citep{zhou2024alignment,arditi2024refusal}; prior reasoning safety work remains at the text level~\citep{harmthoughts,safethink}. The intersection---hidden-state monitoring of reasoning model safety trajectories---is unexplored, and existing hidden-state analyses operate across layers (spatial) rather than across generation steps (temporal).\looseness=-1

We conduct a systematic analysis across four reasoning models, primarily Qwen-based (3/4 models), with one Llama model providing evidence from a second architecture family, at two scales (7--8B, 32B) on the HarmThoughts benchmark. Our central finding is methodological: the choice of layer selection metric entirely determines whether an HS advantage is observed. A composite metric (balanced accuracy $\times$ crossing rate) selects shallow layers for 32B models because shallow representations compress directional information, so a linear probe operates near the noise floor and threshold crossings reflect noise rather than semantic transitions. At these layers, only the two 7--8B models show significant HS advantage.\looseness=-1

Our contributions are:
\begin{itemize}
    \item \textbf{Metric-induced layer selection bias.} Prior work has noted metric sensitivity in probing~\citep{belinkov2022probing}; our contribution is demonstrating a qualitative reversal (significant to non-significant) in a safety-critical application, where the stakes of metric choice are higher than in typical linguistic probing. Crossing-rate composite metrics systematically select shallow layers across all four models (including Llama), reversing HS probe conclusions at 32B scale. The divergence is not gradual: for QwQ-32B, the CR-composite layer (L2, 3\% depth) yields $p{=}0.83$ (non-significant), while the threshold-based layer (L63, 98\% depth) yields $p{<}0.005$, a qualitative reversal, not a quantitative shift. Random-label controls on both architectures confirm the disagreement requires genuine safety labels; the geometric component is Qwen-specific (\cref{sec:layer-results}).

    \item \textbf{Boundary conditions for the HS advantage.} Against 384d MiniLM, the HS advantage is validated via nested 5-fold CV at 7--8B (+20.1 to +21.9pp, HB corrected), significant at QwQ-32B$^\dagger$ (+19.2pp, position-competitive), and exploratory at R1-32B$^\dagger$ (+15.4pp). This advantage is conditional on two partially correlated factors: it diminishes with stronger encoders (1/4 HB under BGE-1024d; PCA capacity matching preserves significance across all four models) and partially overlaps with position (3/4 linear, 2/4 quadratic residualization; \cref{sec:32b-analysis}).

    \item \textbf{Negative results define method boundaries.} No alternative method consistently matches supervised probing (\cref{tab:negative}): BOCPD/CUSUM fail on gradual transitions; Mahalanobis distance finds near-zero separation; RepE is model-dependent; cross-model transfer fails. Control task selectivity (11.1--16.8pp above chance; \cref{app:control}) confirms genuine safety structure.
\end{itemize}

\noindent These findings establish that layer selection metric is an uncontrolled confound in hidden-state safety probing: any study reporting conclusions from a single metric family risks undetected qualitative reversal.\looseness=-1

\section{Introduction}\label{sec:introduction}

Reasoning models such as DeepSeek-R1~\cite{deepseekr1} and QwQ~\cite{qwq} scale inference-time computation through extended chains of thought (CoT). Recent work documents that these models can ``self-jailbreak'': without adversarial input modification, the CoT transitions from safety-aware deliberation to committed harmful generation~\cite{harmthoughts,selfjailbreak}. We define the first reasoning step after which safety deliberation permanently ceases as the \textbf{Safety Commitment Point} (CP). This failure mode differs qualitatively from adversarial jailbreaks on standard LLMs because the harmful transition originates within the model's own reasoning. Recent work shows that chain-of-thought faithfulness is limited~\citep{chen2025unfaithful}, motivating hidden-state monitoring that bypasses surface text. Before retrospective characterization can inform future detection systems, a prior question must be answered: can current probing methods reliably distinguish pre-CP from post-CP reasoning steps, and under what conditions? This paper provides \emph{retrospective} classification (not online detection) of what hidden-state and text-based probes can and cannot detect; false positive rates remain 11--50\%, so deployment applications are future work.\looseness=-1

Existing safety detectors target fundamentally different problems. Hidden-state (HS) methods such as TrajGuard~\cite{trajguard} and SafeSwitch~\cite{safeswitch} classify adversarial inputs at the token level, while text monitors like SafeRemind~\cite{saferemind} scan generated reasoning for explicit violations. Neither tracks the gradual, multi-step commitment process. HS probes require choosing which transformer layer to monitor, a researcher degree of freedom typically treated as a minor implementation detail. Before asking which modality is better, a prior methodological question must be answered: how sensitive are probe conclusions to the choice of layer selection metric? We show this choice alone can reverse a study's central conclusion: the same data yield a 14-layer (R1-8B) to 61-layer (QwQ-32B) divergence depending solely on metric choice; for QwQ-32B, at threshold-based layers the HS advantage is +19pp ($p{<}0.005$); at crossing-rate-selected layers, it is non-significant ($p{=}0.83$). Prior hidden-state probing targets standard LLMs~\citep{zhou2024alignment,arditi2024refusal}; prior reasoning safety work remains at the text level~\citep{harmthoughts,safethink}. The intersection---hidden-state monitoring of reasoning model safety trajectories---is unexplored, and existing hidden-state analyses operate across layers (spatial) rather than across generation steps (temporal).\looseness=-1

We conduct a systematic analysis across four reasoning models, primarily Qwen-based (3/4 models), with one Llama model providing evidence from a second architecture family, at two scales (7--8B, 32B) on the HarmThoughts benchmark. Our central finding is methodological: the choice of layer selection metric entirely determines whether an HS advantage is observed. A composite metric (balanced accuracy $\times$ crossing rate) selects shallow layers for 32B models because shallow representations compress directional information, so a linear probe operates near the noise floor and threshold crossings reflect noise rather than semantic transitions. At these layers, only the two 7--8B models show significant HS advantage.\looseness=-1

Threshold-based metrics (precision, inverse FPR, additive composite) share a common confusion matrix and empirically converge; BA independently confirms deep-layer selection (\cref{tab:layer_selection}). At these layers, the HS advantage is graded: \emph{validated via nested 5-fold CV} at 7--8B (precision +20.1 to +21.9pp; \cref{tab:hs_vs_text}), \emph{significant} but suggestive of position-competitiveness at QwQ-32B$^\dagger$ (+19.2pp; \cref{sec:32b-analysis}), and \emph{exploratory} at R1-32B$^\dagger$ (+15.4pp, pattern consistent with position mediation, below MDE; \cref{sec:experiments}).\looseness=-1

Our contributions are:
\begin{itemize}
    \item \textbf{Metric-induced layer selection bias.} Prior work has noted metric sensitivity in probing~\citep{belinkov2022probing}; our contribution is demonstrating a qualitative reversal (significant to non-significant) in a safety-critical application, where the stakes of metric choice are higher than in typical linguistic probing. Crossing-rate composite metrics systematically select shallow layers across all four models (including Llama), reversing HS probe conclusions at 32B scale. The divergence is not gradual: for QwQ-32B, the CR-composite layer (L2, 3\% depth) yields $p{=}0.83$ (non-significant), while the threshold-based layer (L63, 98\% depth) yields $p{<}0.005$, a qualitative reversal, not a quantitative shift. Random-label controls on both architectures confirm the disagreement requires genuine safety labels; the geometric component is Qwen-specific (\cref{sec:layer-results}).

    \item \textbf{Boundary conditions for the HS advantage.} Against 384d MiniLM, the HS advantage is validated via nested 5-fold CV at 7--8B (+20.1 to +21.9pp, HB corrected), significant at QwQ-32B$^\dagger$ (+19.2pp, position-competitive), and exploratory at R1-32B$^\dagger$ (+15.4pp). This advantage is conditional on two partially correlated factors: it diminishes with stronger encoders (1/4 HB under BGE-1024d; PCA capacity matching preserves significance across all four models) and partially overlaps with position (3/4 linear, 2/4 quadratic residualization; \cref{sec:32b-analysis}).

    \item \textbf{Negative results define method boundaries.} No alternative method consistently matches supervised probing (\cref{tab:negative}): BOCPD/CUSUM fail on gradual transitions; Mahalanobis distance finds near-zero separation; RepE is model-dependent; cross-model transfer fails. Control task selectivity (11.1--16.8pp above chance; \cref{app:control}) confirms genuine safety structure.
\end{itemize}

\noindent These findings establish that layer selection metric is an uncontrolled confound in hidden-state safety probing: any study reporting conclusions from a single metric family risks undetected qualitative reversal.\looseness=-1

lines: Adversarial prompts designed to bypass safety mechanisms (e.g., GCG suffixes) cause the model to skip safety deliberation entirely: 90.4\% of jailbroken traces have CP${=}0$, meaning the model commits to harmful generation from the first reasoning step. This contrasts with HarmThoughts, where non-adversarial prompts trigger extended safety deliberation before commitment (mean relative CP position ${\approx}0.7$). The CP framework is most informative when prompts elicit deliberation that can be monitored; adversarial prompts that circumvent deliberation represent a boundary condition where commitment detection is vacuous. The geometric compression evidence (\cref{tab:cosine_volatility}; volatility ratio $1.67\times$) remains valid because it measures representational properties independent of CP annotations.
+\subsection{AdvBench Layer Selection Bias Replication}
+\label{app:advbench_layer_bias}

+We replicate the five-metric layer selection analysis on AdvBench~\citep{advbench} to test whether metric-induced layer divergence depends on HarmThoughts-specific CP annotations or generalizes to simpler binary supervision. Using R1-8B, we generate reasoning traces for all 520 AdvBench prompts, classify each as jailbreak or safe via keyword matching, and evaluate logistic regression probes across all 32 layers (L0--L31) with windows $W \in \{1, 3, 5, 15\}$. The 60/20/20 train/val/test split matches HarmThoughts protocol.
+\paragraph{Data distribution.} Of 520 traces, 412 (79.2\%) are classified as jailbreak and 108 (20.8\%) as safe.
+\begin{table}[h]
+\centering
+\small
+\caption{AdvBench layer selection (R1-8B, 32 layers). CR-composite selects shallow layers; threshold-based metrics select deep layers, consistent with HarmThoughts (\cref{tab:layer_selection}).}
+\label{tab:advbench_layer_selection}
+\begin{tabular}{lccc}
+\toprule
+\textbf{Metric} & \textbf{Best Layer} & \textbf{Depth (\%)} & \textbf{Best $W$} \\
+\midrule
+CR-composite (BA $\times$ CR) & L9 & 29.0\% & 5 \\
+Inverse FPR & L29 & 93.5\% & 15 \\
+Balanced accuracy & L22 & 71.0\% & 15 \\
+\bottomrule
+\end{tabular}
+\end{table}

+\paragraph{Crossing rate pattern.} Mean crossing rate at shallow layers is elevated relative to deep layers, consistent with the cosine compression range observed on HarmThoughts (\cref{tab:cosine_volatility}).
+\paragraph{Per-window consistency.} Threshold-based metrics consistently select deep layers regardless of window size, while the CR-composite is pulled toward shallow layers across all windows.

+The 13-layer divergence (42\% of model depth) between CR-composite and threshold-based selection replicates the HarmThoughts pattern (L0 vs.\ L14, 44\% divergence) under different label semantics (binary jailbreak/safe vs.\ step-level CP). This confirms that the bias arises from representational geometry (shallow-layer cosine compression) rather than task-specific label structure.
